clue.text: Dope in mess, to an extent

parts.note: a hash is a mess, as in 'make a hash of it'
the suffix -ish means somewhat, to an extent

explanation.surface: Someone has made a mess of things to some extent through drug-taking.
explanation.definitionFit: Dope is slang for cannabis, and hashish is cannabis resin.

clue.text: Underworld boss pleased a henchman keeps up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the letters from bottom to top, backwards
the phrase keeps the answer within its run of letters, like a container holding stock

parts.note: the run of letters across 'pleaSED A Henchman'

explanation.surface: A gangland boss is pleased because his heavy is keeping up appearances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underworld boss' reads as a crime lord, but it means the Greek god who rules the realm of the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Hades is the Greek god who rules the dead, so the boss of the classical underworld.

clue.text: Second criminal is late to leave dock

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so the following letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for second
these six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A second offender is late leaving the dock of a courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's dock is in a courtroom; the definition's dock is a harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship sets sail when it departs from port, which is leaving dock.

clue.text: Holy man in area with border of 0.1 cm

indicators.note: having a border of something means being surrounded by it, so the other piece goes round

parts.note: 0.1 cm is one millimetre, written I (one) and MM
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A holy man stands in a tiny space whose edge is a millimetre wide.
explanation.walkthrough: One millimetre is spelt out as Roman I plus MM, and the area's A sits between the two Ms.
explanation.definitionFit: An imam is the man who leads prayers in a mosque, a Muslim religious leader.

clue.text: Eagles hit a lithe falcon or cuckoo, circling island

indicators.note: circling means going around, so the jumbled letters enclose one more
cuckoo means crazy, so the letters before it go mad and rearrange

parts.note: fourteen letters to be rearranged
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: The Eagles, as birds, attack a lithe falcon, or perhaps a cuckoo, as they circle an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The Eagles are the American rock band, not birds, despite the falcon and cuckoo nearby. The fourteen letters rearrange round I.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotel California is the 1977 title track and best-known single by the Eagles rock band.

clue.text: One running after calories consumed in fat camp

indicators.note: after tells us the running piece follows the rest in order
something consumed in another goes inside it, like food eaten

parts.note: taken as written, to hold the next piece
C is the abbreviation for calories, as on food labels
Roman numeral one
a machine that is running is on

explanation.surface: Someone goes jogging at a weight-loss camp after eating too many calories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat camp' reads as one phrase, but FAT is wordplay and 'camp' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A camp can mean a group within a larger body holding shared views, which is a faction.

clue.text: Nursing head, why I visited tip-top Japanese bar that's exasperating

indicators.note: nursing means holding something close, so the phrase that follows wraps around this word

parts.words: why I visited tip-top Japanese bar
parts.note: the reason for a visit to a Japanese bar would be 'for good sake', the rice wine, with tip-top as GOOD
a ness is a headland, a head of land jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: Someone with a sore head went to a fancy Japanese bar, and is now exasperated.
explanation.walkthrough: Sake is Japanese rice wine; a ness is a headland, common in Scottish place names such as Loch Ness.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an exclamation of impatience or annoyance, used when someone finds a situation exasperating.

clue.text: Classes about, say, boring politicians

parts.note: CA, for circa, means about

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so the short piece goes inside the politicians

parts.note: Tories are members of the UK Conservative Party
e.g. means for example, which 'say' can mean

explanation.surface: Groups of boring politicians, say, are discussed.
explanation.definitionFit: Classes and categories are both groups into which things are sorted by type.

clue.text: Assigned current Express journalist to take minutes

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so the minutes go inside the earlier pieces

parts.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current
to put something is to express it, as in 'put it plainly'
ED is short for editor
M is the abbreviation for minutes

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor sends a journalist to take minutes at a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: The Express is a British newspaper, but here 'Express' is a verb. The M slots in after I.
explanation.definitionFit: To impute is to attribute or assign something, often blame, to someone.

clue.text: Eschewer of responsibility jailed by loveless tyrant

indicators.note: someone jailed by another is locked up inside them
love is zero in tennis, a round letter, so loveless means that letter is removed

parts.note: Nero was the notoriously cruel Roman emperor
an onus is a burden or responsibility

explanation.surface: Someone who avoids responsibility is locked up by a heartless dictator.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is tennis for zero, the round letter, which the Roman emperor loses before enclosing the burden.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonuser is someone who abstains from using something, so an eschewer of it.

clue.text: Person knocking frame of durable vehicle

indicators.note: a frame is the edge around something, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of durable
a tractor is a farm vehicle

explanation.surface: Someone is knocking against the frame of a sturdy vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: To knock is to criticise, so a person knocking things is a critic or detractor.

clue.text: How toccata starts with a lot of piano playing? It's easy to score

indicators.note: how a word starts points to its opening letter only

parts.note: first letter of toccata

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are played about with and moved around
a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the last letter goes

parts.note: taken as written, before being cut short

explanation.surface: A question about how a toccata begins: with lots of piano playing?
explanation.walkthrough: The musical surface hides a football definition. Drop the final O of piano and rearrange the rest after T.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a tap-in is a goal scored with a simple short touch from very close range.

clue.text: See 24
It's risky to open these tuck boxes left by mogul

indicators.note: something that boxes another encloses it, as a box holds its contents

parts.note: tuck is British school slang for food, especially snacks
L is the abbreviation for left
Bill Gates, the Microsoft tycoon

explanation.surface: A schoolchild's tuck box left beside a tycoon might be risky to open.
explanation.walkthrough: A tuck box is the chest of snacks a British boarding-school pupil keeps.
explanation.definitionFit: Opening the floodgates is an idiom for unleashing something uncontrollable, so they are risky to open.

clue.text: Wanting top, perhaps Indian setter used for building motivation

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, and in a down clue the top is the first letter, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: a Hindu is an example of an Indian, hence 'perhaps'
cement sets hard and is used in construction

explanation.surface: A crossword setter from India, who lacks a hat, is motivated by building something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' tempts toward a crossword compiler or a dog; here it is something that sets, the building material.
explanation.definitionFit: An inducement is an incentive, something offered to motivate a person to act.

clue.text: Russian who worked in bars walking unsteadily, putting away whiskey

indicators.note: unsteadily suggests staggering about, so the letters lurch out of order
putting something away removes it from view, so that letter leaves the word

parts.note: taken as written
whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A Russian who drinks in bars walks unsteadily after knocking back whiskey.
explanation.walkthrough: The bars are musical bars, not pubs: remove W from WALKING and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Mikhail Glinka was a nineteenth-century Russian composer, and composers work in musical bars.

clue.text: Person scoffing articles in Gasthof around 1

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the paired words go either side of the number

parts.note: der is a German definite article, and a Gasthof is a German inn, so two of them
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone is scoffing articles in a German inn around one o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: '1' looks like a cross-reference to 1 Across, but it is simply the number one. 'Gasthof' signals German.
explanation.definitionFit: A derider is someone who mocks or ridicules, a scoffer.

clue.text: They get reactions from version of litmus paper

indicators.note: a version of something is a reworked form of it, so the letters come in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the i is a British national newspaper

explanation.surface: Litmus paper is used in chemistry to get colour reactions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litmus paper' reads as one item, but paper is the British newspaper called i.
explanation.definitionFit: Stimuli are things that provoke responses, so they get reactions from organisms.

clue.text: Primate is upset by e.g. bishop wearing silver

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the word reads from the bottom

parts.note: the word is, turned around

indicators.note: a piece wearing another is clothed in it, so it sits inside

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a bishop is an example of a chess man

explanation.surface: A primate is upset by a bishop wearing silver vestments.
explanation.walkthrough: The bishop is a chess piece, a man, rather than a clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: The siamang is a large black gibbon of Southeast Asia, a primate.

clue.text: All told Greek character pens books on line

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, as animals in a pen, so the books go inside

parts.note: iota is a letter of the Greek alphabet
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Altogether, a Greek author writes books online.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' looks like 'writes'; here it means encloses. 'On' places L after the rest in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: All told and in total are both idioms meaning counting everything, altogether.

clue.text: Is it a page from an e-book, really?

parts.note: the e of e-book, as in electronic
a verso is the left-hand page of a book

explanation.surface: A puzzled reader asks whether this is really a page from an e-book.
explanation.walkthrough: Whimsically, an e-book page would be an e-verso, as a paper book has recto and verso pages.
explanation.definitionFit: Ever so is an informal intensifier meaning very or really, as in 'ever so kind'.

clue.text: Understood philosopher's works

parts.note: to see is to understand, as in 'I see'
John Stuart Mill, the English philosopher; the 's joins him to the definition

explanation.surface: Someone has grasped a philosopher's writings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' looks like a philosopher's writings; it is the industrial sense, a factory.
explanation.definitionFit: A works is a factory or industrial site, and a sawmill is a plant where timber is cut.

clue.text: If all else fails, ambassador cuts a dry sausage, as some say,

indicators.note: a piece that cuts into others breaks in between them

parts.note: taken as written
TT, teetotal, means abstaining from alcohol

indicators.note: says how some people pronounce a word, with a German W sounded like V

parts.note: wurst is German for sausage
HE is His or Her Excellency, the title of an ambassador

explanation.surface: As a last resort, an ambassador slices up some dry sausage.
explanation.walkthrough: HE breaks into A TT plus WORST.
explanation.definitionFit: At the worst is an idiom meaning if the worst comes to it, if everything else goes wrong.

clue.text: Do butterfly's wings in shadow start to interest Mike?

indicators.note: wings are the two sides of something, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of shadow

indicators.note: the start of a word is just its opening letter

parts.note: first letter of interest
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Would the sight of a butterfly's wings in shadow catch Mike's interest?
explanation.walkthrough: The butterfly looks like an insect, but it is a swimming stroke; the question mark flags butterfly as just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Butterfly is a swimming stroke, so doing butterfly is one way to swim.

clue.text: Crikey! Covers of Marley track turned up

indicators.note: the covers of a book are its front and back, so only the outer letters count

parts.note: first and last letters of Marley

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means flipped to read upwards, backwards

parts.note: to dog someone is to track or follow them

explanation.surface: An excited fan finds cover versions of a Bob Marley track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covers' and 'track' sound musical, but one picks the outer letters and the other is a verb meaning follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Crikey and my God are both exclamations of surprise or shock.

clue.text: You picked up capsized boater, possibly in a state

indicators.note: something picked up is caught by the ear, so the sound counts

parts.note: the letter U is pronounced like the word you

indicators.note: a capsized boat is upside down, so in a down clue the word is flipped

parts.note: a boater is a straw hat, hence 'possibly' marking an example

explanation.surface: A rescuer picks up a capsized boater who is in a bad state.
explanation.walkthrough: The boater looks like someone in a boat, but it is a flat straw hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Utah is one of the fifty states of the USA.

clue.text: Jazz bandleader's skill that is followed by playwright

parts.note: art means skill, as in 'the art of persuasion'
i.e. is short for id est, that is
George Bernard Shaw, the Irish playwright

explanation.surface: A jazz bandleader's talent is followed by a dramatist.
explanation.definitionFit: Artie Shaw was an American clarinettist who led a big band in the swing era.

clue.text: Ultimately stubborn sod, ruler loses face in tragedy, almost

indicators.note: losing face means losing the front, so the first letter is dropped
ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: last letter of stubborn
sod is turf, a piece of earth
a king is a ruler

explanation.surface: A stubborn ruler is humiliated in what is nearly a tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sod' looks like an insult, but it means turf. 'Almost' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A near thing is a narrow escape, something that was almost a disaster.

clue.text: Incredibly animated lady had meal during jamboree

indicators.note: something happening during an event falls within it, so it goes inside

parts.note: a gala is a festive celebration
to have a meal is to eat, past tense

explanation.surface: An extraordinarily lively woman had dinner at a big party.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the sculptor Pygmalion's statue came to life, later named Galatea; 'incredibly' marks the miracle.
explanation.definitionFit: Galatea is the ivory statue that came alive in the Pygmalion myth, a lady brought to life against all belief.

clue.text: Perhaps made pants well worn by old daughter

indicators.note: something worn by another is covered by it, so it sits inside

parts.note: ex means former, old
D is the abbreviation for daughter
hale means healthy, well

explanation.surface: An old daughter perhaps made underpants that were well worn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like underwear, but it is the verb, to breathe heavily; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Panting is breathing out heavily, so having panted is one way of having exhaled.
